name: Othello
kicker: Shakespeare’s tragedy of the Moor of Venice · Jealousy turned fatal
briefing: A celebrated Venetian general secretly marries Desdemona, the woman he loves, only to watch his own trusted officer poison his mind with jealousy. Using nothing but a dropped handkerchief and a string of lies, the villain Iago convinces the general that his new wife has betrayed him. By the play’s final scene, Shakespeare’s study of jealousy has destroyed nearly everyone on stage.
accept: the tragedy of othello the moor of venice

qb.tip: Only 2 Middle School/Easy High School tossups exist; 8 more real tossups turned up at Regular High School difficulty, so this sample leans harder on that pool than most topics.

sample.note: 10 real QBReader tossups (2 Middle School/Easy High School + 8 Regular High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: Brabantio accuses this man of using witchcraft to win his daughter’s heart, but the Venetian Senate lets their marriage stand after hearing the couple describe their courtship. The Senate then sends this man to defend Cyprus from a Turkish fleet that a storm destroys before any battle begins.
tossups.r: This man’s ensign tricks him into believing his bride has betrayed him using a dropped handkerchief as false proof. For 10 points, name this Shakespearean general who smothers his wife Desdemona in a jealous rage.

tossups.p: This man explains to the Venetian Senate that he won his wife’s love only through stories of his travels and battles, not through sorcery. His ensign resents being passed over for a promotion that instead goes to a less experienced officer named Cassio.
tossups.r: That ensign gets Cassio drunk and provokes a brawl that costs Cassio his rank. For 10 points, name this Shakespearean tragic hero, a Venetian general undone by jealousy.

tossups.p: A rejected suitor named Roderigo pays this man’s scheming ensign for help winning the woman this man has just married. That ensign later convinces Cassio to beg this man’s wife to plead his case, then twists their private meetings into “evidence” of an affair.
tossups.r: This man was given a handkerchief, supposedly woven by a sibyl and dyed in mummy, which he passed on to his wife as his first gift to her. For 10 points, name this general who demands his wife produce that handkerchief as proof of her faithfulness.

tossups.p: This man’s wife drops an heirloom handkerchief, which her attendant Emilia finds and gives to her own husband without realizing his intentions. That husband plants the handkerchief in Cassio’s room, and Cassio passes it on to his mistress, Bianca.
tossups.r: This man watches a conversation between Cassio and Iago that he is tricked into believing is about his own wife. For 10 points, name this jealous Shakespearean general.

tossups.p: In one scene, this man’s ensign warns him to beware “the green-eyed monster,” feeding suspicions that his wife has been unfaithful. That ensign had earlier wondered aloud in a soliloquy, “And what’s he then that says I play the villain?”
tossups.r: Consumed by jealousy, this man strikes his wife in public and calls her foul names in front of a visiting Venetian nobleman. For 10 points, name this Shakespearean general who later smothers that wife in their bed.

tossups.p: Before her death, this man’s wife sings a sad song that she learned from her mother’s maid, Barbary. This man’s ensign had earlier convinced a rejected suitor named Roderigo to ambush the newly demoted Cassio.
tossups.r: That ensign then killed Roderigo to silence him. For 10 points, name this Shakespearean general who smothers his own wife, Desdemona, believing she betrayed him.

tossups.p: After this man kills his wife, Emilia bursts in and reveals that she unknowingly gave the fatal handkerchief to her husband, exposing his lies. Iago stabs Emilia to keep her quiet, but the truth still reaches this man.
tossups.r: Realizing his fatal mistake, this man delivers a final speech recalling his years of service before killing himself with a hidden weapon. For 10 points, name this tragic Shakespearean general, the title character of a play set partly in Cyprus.

tossups.p: This man’s new bride is the daughter of a Venetian senator named Brabantio, who is said to have died of grief over the marriage before the play ends. A Venetian nobleman named Lodovico later arrives from Venice carrying letters that recall this man and name Cassio governor of Cyprus.
tossups.r: This man had governed Cyprus after replacing a man named Montano. For 10 points, name this Shakespearean general whose ensign Iago destroys his marriage out of resentment.

tossups.p: This man’s final speech recalls killing a Turk who had beaten a Venetian in the city of Aleppo. Before that, this man’s loyal lieutenant Cassio was demoted after a drunken brawl engineered by this man’s ensign.
tossups.r: This man was falsely convinced that his wife Desdemona had been unfaithful with that same lieutenant. For 10 points, name this Shakespearean general who smothers his wife and then takes his own life.

tossups.p: The actor Paul Robeson famously played the title role of this play on Broadway in a landmark production. This play’s plot is thought to be based on an Italian tale sometimes called “A Moorish Captain,” by the writer Cinthio [“SIN-tee-oh”].
tossups.r: Its main character is convinced by a dropped handkerchief that his wife has betrayed him. For 10 points, name this Shakespearean tragedy whose jealous general smothers his wife, Desdemona.

tossups.p: This play’s villain, an ensign passed over for a promotion, recruits a rejected suitor named Roderigo to help ruin the marriage at this play’s center. That villain’s own wife, Emilia, unknowingly hands him the handkerchief that seals the tragedy.
tossups.r: This play’s protagonist smothers his wife in their bed after being deceived by that ensign. For 10 points, name this Shakespearean tragedy set partly in Venice and partly in Cyprus.

tossups.p: In this play, a Venetian senator named Brabantio accuses the protagonist of using witchcraft to win his daughter’s love. A storm destroys an invading Turkish fleet early in this play, shifting its focus away from war and toward the protagonist’s marriage.
tossups.r: The protagonist’s ensign convinces him that his bride has been unfaithful with his own lieutenant, Cassio. For 10 points, name this Shakespearean tragedy whose title general smothers his wife, Desdemona.

tossups.p: This play’s villain gets the protagonist’s lieutenant drunk, provoking a brawl that costs him his rank and sets the villain’s revenge in motion. That villain later tells the protagonist to beware “the green-eyed monster” of jealousy.
tossups.r: The protagonist’s wife is smothered after a dropped handkerchief convinces him of her guilt. For 10 points, name this Shakespearean tragedy featuring a scheming ensign who destroys his general’s marriage.

tossups.p: This play’s subplot follows a jilted suitor named Roderigo, who pays the villain for help and is later killed by him to cover his tracks. The villain’s wife, Emilia, is murdered after she exposes her husband’s scheme to the protagonist.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Shakespearean tragedy in which a Venetian general smothers his wife after believing his ensign’s lies about her faithfulness.

tossups.p: Early in this play, the protagonist defends his marriage before the Venetian Senate after his new father-in-law accuses him of sorcery. Its villain is driven partly by resentment at being passed over for a promotion given to a less experienced officer, Cassio.
tossups.r: Its heroine, Desdemona, is smothered in her bed after a missing handkerchief convinces her husband of her unfaithfulness. For 10 points, name this Shakespearean tragedy, perhaps literature’s most famous study of jealousy.

clues.t: Smothers his wife, Desdemona, in their bed after being deceived about her faithfulness
A tragedy by William Shakespeare, first performed in 1604
His ensign, Iago, manipulates him into a jealous rage out of resentment and ambition
A dropped handkerchief is used as false proof that his wife has been unfaithful
After learning the truth, he kills himself with a hidden weapon
Cassio, a less experienced officer, is promoted to lieutenant over Iago, fueling Iago’s resentment
Set partly in Venice and partly in Cyprus, where he governs after replacing Montano
Brabantio, his wife’s father, accuses him of witchcraft before the Venetian Senate
Emilia, Iago’s wife, unknowingly gives him the handkerchief, then is killed after exposing his scheme
Iago gets his lieutenant drunk, provoking a brawl that costs the man his military rank
A rejected suitor, Roderigo, pays Iago for help and is later killed by him
Iago warns him to beware “the green-eyed monster” of jealousy
He defends himself before the Senate by explaining he won his wife through stories of his travels, not sorcery
A storm destroys an invading Turkish fleet near Cyprus before any battle is fought
Cassio gives the planted handkerchief to his mistress, Bianca, unaware of Iago’s trap
His wife sings a sad song she learned from her mother’s maid, Barbary, shortly before her death
In a soliloquy, Iago wonders, “And what’s he then that says I play the villain?”
Consumed by jealousy, he strikes his wife and calls her foul names in front of the visiting Venetian Lodovico
The actor Paul Robeson famously played the title role in a landmark Broadway production
The plot is thought to come from an Italian tale sometimes called “A Moorish Captain,” by the writer Cinthio
His final speech recalls killing a Turk who had beaten a Venetian in the city of Aleppo
His wife’s father, Brabantio, is said to have died of grief over the marriage

trap.title: Othello or Iago?
trap.body: Most of this tossup’s clues describe scheming, lying, and manipulating — planting the handkerchief, stoking jealousy, destroying a marriage. Those are all things the villain Iago does, not the title character, so “Iago” is the single most tempting wrong buzz on this line.
trap.fix: Ask who the clue is happening TO, not who is doing the scheming. A clue about someone being deceived, growing jealous, or smothering his wife is about the general; save “Iago” for clues that describe the schemer himself.
trap.line: Real answer line: Othello, the Moor of Venice.
